title: Guardrails and Failure Containment
html:
Guardrails and Failure Containment

Baodium’s checkout measurements helped engineers locate slow operations. The same measurements could diagnose overload in the search application, but the team still needed controls to prevent heavy work from consuming capacity reserved for customer searches. Admission limits determine which requests may reach a constrained dependency and whether excess requests are rejected, deferred, or answered through an approved fallback.

Customers find products on Baodium through storefront search, which also offers suggestions as they type. Both features run in the search application, which sends queries to a shared search cluster through a single client and worker pool. When the team later built catalog export, which lets a merchant download every product listing as a spreadsheet, it reused the same client and pool, because an export is essentially a series of searches.

As merchants began exporting larger catalogs, customer searches slowed down, and the dashboards from Chapter 8 identified two causes. During the slowest periods, six exports were running at once, each holding a worker for several seconds and issuing one cluster query per page of results, while the worker pool’s queue held as many as 40 waiting customer searches. Most of each search’s extra delay, roughly 400 milliseconds at the 95th percentile, was spent in that queue, but query time inside the cluster had also risen from about 60 to 150 milliseconds, because the exports had multiplied the number of queries it received. The shared limit allowed an export to consume hundreds of times more backend execution time than a search without any separate allocation for the customer-facing workload.

The team considered adding workers and shortening export timeouts. More workers would shorten the queue, but they would also let more export queries reach a cluster that was already slowing down. A shorter export timeout would cut long downloads short, yet the exports that remained would keep sending the same queries. The team needed two separate controls, one deciding which work could occupy the application’s workers and another capping how much of the cluster each workload could use. The team first separated worker allocations from backend-query limits. Later failures required a queue for long exports, a circuit breaker and rate limits for general cluster slowdown, and a staged recovery procedure. The rules for operations that change state required additional care, because a refused request and an operation whose response was lost have different recovery requirements.

Workload Separation

A limit can protect a resource only if it tracks the work that consumes that resource, so we begin by looking at what each workload costs. An interactive search returns one bounded page while a customer waits, whereas an export retrieves many pages and writes them to a file that the merchant downloads later, as Table \(\ref{tab:search-workloads}\) shows.

Because of that difference, a limit on incoming HTTP requests would treat a search and an export as equal, when in fact one export can issue hundreds of cluster queries after its HTTP request has completed. The team therefore split admission into two decisions. The first decides whether an export job may start, which bounds how many exports run at once. The second decides whether a running job may send its next query, which bounds how much of the cluster exports consume. Checking each page separately also makes cancellation effective, because a canceled export stops before its next page instead of working through the rest of the catalog.

Exports also needed somewhere to run, and the team first considered keeping one worker pool and letting customer searches go to the front of its queue. That shortens the wait for searches already in the queue, but it does nothing about workers that exports are holding for several seconds each, so a burst of exports can fill the pool anyway. Instead, exports got their own bounded executor. A separate executor sits partly idle when no exports are running, but it guarantees that exports never occupy the workers that serve customers, and the team considered that guarantee worth the idle capacity. The export-job limit is checked before a job enters that executor’s queue, because a job that waited for a permit inside the executor would hold a queue entry and memory while it waited, recreating the original queueing problem one level down.

Bulkheads and Resource Reservations

A separate executor solved the queueing problem but not the cluster problem, because export workers and search workers query the same cluster. A ship’s hull is divided by walls called bulkheads into watertight compartments, so that a breach floods one compartment rather than the whole ship. A software bulkhead applies the same idea by limiting how much of a shared resource one workload can occupy. In the search application, every export query must hold two permits, one from a small export allowance and one from the process’s pool of backend-call slots, as Figure \(\ref{fig:ch09-bulkhead}\) shows.

Suppose each process has eight backend-call slots and exports may hold at most two of them. Exports can then never occupy more than two slots, and customer searches can use all eight whenever exports are idle. The export allowance is a ceiling rather than a reservation, which means that under sustained customer traffic, exports could wait indefinitely. If exports had to finish by a deadline, the team would need to reserve slots for them and accept that customer searches might be refused while reserved slots sat unused. Merchants could tolerate slower exports, but customers would not tolerate slower searches, which made the ceiling the right choice.

Releasing the permit between pages is what makes the ceiling effective. Each export worker acquires a permit, retrieves one page, releases the permit, and only then writes the page to its output file, so while the file is being written, the released slot can serve a customer search instead of sitting unused for several seconds. The cost is one permit acquisition per page, which is negligible beside the query itself. Buffering every page in memory and writing the file at the end avoids even that cost, but a large catalog can exhaust the application’s memory, so each worker streams pages to bounded temporary storage instead.

Choosing a First Limit

The numbers eight and two began as estimates, which the team then put to a test. Because the limit under consideration was the number of backend calls that exports may hold, the test varied only that number. Eight export jobs were kept queued, the same customer searches, suggestions, and catalog sizes ran in every trial, and only the number of export permits changed between trials, with the results shown in Table \(\ref{tab:export-concurrency-test}\).

With a search target of 300 milliseconds at the 95th percentile, two permits is the best of the three settings. Raising the limit from two to four adds two completed exports per minute but pushes search latency to 680 milliseconds, because the additional export queries compete with searches inside the cluster. Before production, two permits also had to meet the search target with larger catalogs, uneven traffic across instances, and one instance unavailable. A limit chosen this way can be defended in a way that a rule of thumb, such as reserving a fixed percentage of the pool, cannot, because the team knows what the limit achieves and which measurement would justify changing it.

Limits Across the Fleet

Every number so far applies to one process, while the cluster receives the combined traffic of all of them. Four processes that each permit two export calls can send eight export calls at once, a rolling deployment that briefly adds a fifth process raises that number to ten, and indexing jobs and administration tools query the cluster as well. The team therefore worked down from the cluster’s tested capacity and recorded the reason for each step, as Table \(\ref{tab:search-allocation}\) shows.

Laying the numbers out in this order shows which values depend on which measurements. If the deployment surge grew from five processes to six, for instance, eight slots per process would consume the entire allowance of 48 and leave no margin, so each process would drop to seven slots, two for exports and five for customer searches alone. The reservation of 16 queries for background callers depends equally on those callers, because nothing in the search application can stop them from exceeding it. Baodium therefore limits the indexing service to 12 concurrent queries and the administration tools to 4, each enforced by the caller, so that together they never exceed 16.

The application’s share can be divided among processes either as fixed shares or through a coordinated allocation. Fixed shares are simpler to operate but leave capacity unused when traffic is uneven across instances. A coordinated allocation uses capacity more fully, but it adds a dependency and requires a policy for when coordination fails, because a process that kept using an expired share could overlap with another process using the same capacity. Baodium chose fixed shares, since four instances rarely receive highly uneven traffic, and the cost of a little unused capacity was smaller than the cost of another dependency in the admission path.

Queueing and Deferred Work

The bulkhead protected customer searches, but it lengthened large exports to several minutes, and an HTTP request held open for that long was unreliable, because any network interruption lost the download. Because merchants did not need an export to finish within one request, the team changed submission to return a job reference as soon as the job was durably accepted. The merchant now checks progress and downloads the file when it is ready. In exchange, the team took on a job store, a status endpoint, and cleanup of finished files, a cost it accepted because each additional piece was simple and the download no longer depended on one long connection.

A queue of accepted jobs needs a limit of its own, and storage capacity is a poor basis for it, because a durable queue can hold far more work than the application can finish in an acceptable time. If the tested completion rate is about 20 comparable exports per minute, a backlog of 100 jobs means that newly accepted work waits roughly five minutes before starting, even with no further arrivals, and larger jobs or fewer workers extend that wait. The admission limit is therefore set from the export completion time that Baodium promises merchants, and the dashboard shows the age of the oldest queued job and the estimated completion delay beside queue depth. Unusually large catalogs go to a separate job class, because otherwise a few of them could occupy every worker while many small exports waited behind them.

An accepted job needs a durable identity, an owner, a status, and a recovery path in case its worker fails, and an application that cannot record those cannot truthfully report the job as accepted. When the backlog reaches its limit, a new submission receives an explicit temporary refusal, and a repeated submission for an accepted job returns that job’s status instead of creating a copy. Chapter 12 examines durable delivery in detail, but for guardrails the essential point is that accepting a job creates an obligation to finish, cancel, or explicitly fail it. A queue cannot serve as a way to report success while work accumulates.

::: decision

**Two slots or six?**

Each search application process has eight backend-call slots, and exports may hold at most two of them. A merchant complains that a catalog export now takes eleven minutes instead of four, and an engineer proposes raising the export allocation to six slots during off-peak hours, arguing that interactive traffic is low at 03:00 anyway.

**Raise the export allocation to six during off-peak hours.**

**Keep the allocation at two and add more export workers.**

**Keep the allocation at two and give exports their own search replica.**

—

A can work, but only with a safeguard decided in advance, because the off-peak assumption will sometimes be wrong. A promotion, customers in other time zones, or a retry storm from a daytime region can all bring interactive traffic into the window, and an allocation based on the clock has no way to detect them. If you choose this option, tie the allocation to measured interactive demand rather than to the time of day, and keep a floor of slots that exports can never take.

B does not increase export throughput, because the two backend permits are the limiting resource. Adding workers that compete for the same two permits completes the same amount of work, with more workers waiting.

C gives exports their own replica and query allocation, which removes direct competition for interactive query slots at the cost of another replica to operate and keep updated. Shared indexing, storage, or network capacity can connect the two workloads even then. This option fits when measured export demand cannot be met within the shared allocation without degrading interactive response times.

:::

Circuit Breakers

A few weeks after these changes, an index rebuild left the search cluster slow for every caller for several minutes. The bulkhead offered no protection, because no single workload was crowding out the others. The search application kept sending queries to an overloaded cluster, each query added to the overload, and each customer search spent its deadline waiting for a response that was likely to fail. A circuit breaker, named after the electrical device, addresses both problems. It records the results of recent calls and, when too many fail or run slowly, stops sending calls for a period, which reduces the load on the dependency while it recovers and lets callers fail in milliseconds instead of waiting out their deadlines. Figure \(\ref{fig:ch09-breaker}\) shows its three states and the conditions under which it changes state.

Closed.

Calls are permitted, and their results are recorded.

Open.

Calls are refused for a configured interval.

Half-open.

A limited number of probe calls test whether normal admission can resume.

For search, the breaker counts transport failures, timeouts, and responses slower than the caller’s allocated time. An empty result is a valid answer, not a dependency failure, so it does not count. While the breaker is open, export workers reschedule their next query according to the job policy instead of polling the breaker, and customer searches receive the supported unavailable response or the fallback described later in the chapter.

Choosing Thresholds

A breaker that opens too readily turns ordinary noise into an outage, and one that opens too slowly provides no protection, so each threshold has to be set against the cluster’s normal behavior. In this example, an interactive search call may take at most 400 milliseconds, or less if the caller’s deadline is shorter, and after reviewing representative successful calls, the engineers chose 250 milliseconds as the slow-call threshold. Listing \(\ref{lst:ch09-breaker}\) shows the resulting policy for one process.

[
  caption={Example local breaker policy for interactive search.},
  label={lst:ch09-breaker}
]
attempt:
  maximum_duration_ms: 400

breaker:
  sample_window_seconds: 20
  minimum_completed_calls: 100
  technical_failure_rate: 0.50
  slow_call_duration_ms: 250
  slow_call_rate: 0.30
  open_interval_seconds: 10
  half_open_calls: 3
  half_open_successes_required: 3

Each process handles about 25 interactive search calls per second, so a 20-second window holds about 500 calls, and the minimum of 100 completed calls is reached in about four seconds at that rate. Without a minimum, a handful of failures during light traffic would produce a large percentage and open the breaker for no reason. In normal operation, fewer than 0.5 percent of calls fail, so a 50 percent failure threshold can be reached only by a condition that affects most calls to the cluster. Similarly, about 2 percent of successful calls normally exceed 250 milliseconds, so a 30 percent slow-call rate is fifteen times the baseline. Export page retrieval normally takes longer than a search, so exports need their own latency threshold, because combining the two workloads under one threshold could open the breaker during ordinary export activity.

The 10-second open interval came from earlier incidents, in which cluster overload had lasted between 5 and 30 seconds, and a slight random variation across processes keeps their probes from arriving together. Because the rebuild lasted far longer than those episodes, the breaker cycled repeatedly through opening, probing, and reopening, and that cycling kept most of the load off the cluster until the rebuild finished. A longer interval suits an outage of that length, but it keeps search unavailable longer than necessary during the far more frequent short episodes, and for that reason the team kept 10 seconds. The breaker also does not wait for its full window, because once the minimum sample exists, it evaluates its thresholds as each result arrives. Calls that have not yet completed contribute no result, however, so in the first seconds of a slowdown, before the breaker has evidence, the concurrency limits are the only protection the cluster has.

Half-Open Probes and Recovery

A half-open probe should exercise the operation that failed, so the search probe is an ordinary bounded query rather than a request to a health endpoint that shows only that the process responds. Three successful probes are weak evidence of full recovery, because three calls say nothing about how the cluster behaves under full load. The breaker therefore closes into the same concurrency limits as before, and the team resumes export processing in stages, checking search latency and export completion between increases, because queued exports and delayed retries released all at once could recreate the overload. Probes also multiply across the fleet, and restarting a process resets most local breaker implementations, so a fleet that restarts repeatedly during an outage sends repeated waves of calls to a failing dependency. The recovery tests described at the end of the chapter include that case.

Rate Limits and Retry Budgets

While investigating the rebuild, the team looked at where the cluster’s load was coming from, and two findings led to the next controls. Both involve rate limits, which are easy to confuse with the concurrency limits we have used so far. Think of a stadium entrance, where the number of people allowed inside at once is a concurrency limit and the number allowed through the turnstiles each minute is a rate limit. A concurrency limit bounds how much work is outstanding, whereas a rate limit bounds how often new attempts begin. Neither replaces the other, because a few slots can issue many requests per second to a fast cluster, while a permitted request rate can exhaust those slots once responses slow down.

Burst Allowance

Rate limits are usually implemented as a token bucket, which admits an attempt by consuming a token and adds tokens at a configured rate, up to a maximum balance. A refill rate of 100 tokens per second with a maximum balance of 10, for instance, permits an immediate burst of 10 attempts followed by further attempts as tokens are added, so it allows up to about 110 calls in a single second rather than a strict 100. The balance should match a burst that the cluster can absorb without unacceptable queueing. Raising it because clients dislike rejection concentrates more work into the same short interval, which defeats the purpose of the limit.

Choosing the Rate-Limit Key

The first finding concerned a merchant integration. Besides the storefront and exports, the search application serves a merchant search API that merchants’ own systems call, and one large merchant was polling its listings through eight API keys at a combined 400 requests per second, roughly a quarter of the cluster’s query load. Limiting that traffic raised the central question in rate limiting, which is whose bucket each request draws from, because the answer determines whether one caller can exhaust an allowance meant for everyone. Each of the four candidate keys produces a distinct outcome for this merchant.

Per IP address.

Many customers share carrier and corporate addresses, and an integration can rotate addresses, so this key measures network location rather than the caller.

Per API key.

At 50 requests per second per key, the merchant’s eight keys admitted all 400 requests, and every additional key raises the allowance by another 50.

Per merchant.

The server resolves each key to its merchant and charges the merchant’s bucket. At 20 requests per second with a burst of 40, the integration received 20 requests per second, and other merchants kept their share.

Fleet-wide per operation class.

This key protects the cluster’s total allowance, but on its own it lets the largest caller take most of that allowance.

Baodium uses two keys together, and a request must pass both. The per-merchant bucket provides fairness among merchants, and the fleet-wide bucket protects the cluster, because many merchants who each remain within their quota can together exceed what the cluster can serve. Retries are charged to the same merchant bucket as first attempts, so a client that retries aggressively spends its own allowance rather than its neighbors’. The merchant identity comes from the authenticated key on the server, never from a field the client supplies, because a client could otherwise claim to be another merchant. Exports follow the same pattern, with a per-merchant quota on accepted jobs and a backend limit that counts calls from every merchant.

Retries as Additional Load

The second finding was that retries had increased the load on the cluster during the rebuild. The search client retried every timed-out call once, so when 20 percent of 100 first attempts per second timed out, the cluster received 120 attempts per second, a 20 percent increase at the moment it had the least spare capacity. A retry budget limits retries to a fraction of recent first attempts. At 5 percent, it permits about five retries per second at that rate, and the remaining candidates receive the configured failure response. The trade-off is deliberate, because although some requests that a retry would have rescued now fail, the cluster is spared extra load at the point where that load does the most damage. The budget also needs a maximum balance and an accounting interval, because credit saved during hours of healthy traffic could otherwise fund a large burst of retries during an outage.

Backoff and jitter spread retries over time but do not limit how many occur, which means they complement a retry budget rather than replace it. Each retry must also fit within the caller’s deadline and pass the breaker, rate, and concurrency checks. The team made the search client the only layer allowed to retry and confirmed that the gateway and SDK added no retries of their own, because two layers that each retry twice can turn one request into nine attempts instead of the three the engineer intended. No backend-call slot is held during backoff, and an export worker returns its job to a scheduled state rather than occupying a worker while it waits.

Fallbacks and Load Shedding

With the cluster protected, the team turned to what customers should receive when a search could not be served. One proposal was to query the primary product database whenever search was unavailable. A fallback helps only if the application can produce it during the failure it is meant to handle, and this one sends every refused search to a database that has never been tested with that workload, which spreads the failure to a second system. Most fallbacks draw on some other resource in this way, and the question to ask of any fallback is which resource it consumes and whether that resource has capacity to spare during the same failure. The team chose a narrower fallback, returning a recent cached result for popular queries and an explicit temporary-unavailable response for everything else, because unrelated results, or an empty list that implies no matching products exist, would mislead the customer.

Load shedding means dropping, refusing, or deferring work that the application is allowed to omit when demand exceeds capacity, and the work worth shedding is the work that consumes the constrained resource. If the cluster is the bottleneck, pausing export queries helps, but disabling an analytics task that never queries the cluster frees no search capacity. For the same reason, a shedding order is defined per resource and enforced where that resource is admitted. CPU scheduling priority cannot substitute for it, because a low-priority thread that has acquired a search slot keeps the slot until it finishes.

Suggestions complicated the earlier arithmetic, because they query the cluster too. If suggestions could take shared slots freely, two exports and three suggestions could leave only three of the eight slots for customer searches. The team therefore turned the export permit into an optional-work permit that exports and suggestions share, so that together they never occupy more than two slots. Before adopting it, the team reran the concurrency test with both workloads drawing on the same two permits. Search latency met its target, fewer than 1 percent of suggestion requests were omitted at peak, and export throughput fell from about 21 to about 18 jobs per minute, which the export completion target could absorb. Listing \(\ref{lst:ch09-shedding}\) shows the resulting admission configuration for each process.

[
  caption={Admission and shedding policy for the search cluster, per process.},
  label={lst:ch09-shedding}]
search_cluster_admission:
  shared_slots: 8
  optional_work_slots: 2        # exports and suggestions combined
  interactive_search:
    uses: any free shared slot  # 6 are never used by optional work
    when_full: queue_250ms_then_retry_later
  search_suggestions:
    admit_while_slots_in_use_below: 6
    when_refused: omit_module
  merchant_export:
    admit_while_slots_in_use_below: 5
    when_refused: defer_job

Optional work can occupy at most two of the eight slots, which leaves at least six that it never uses, while customer searches may take any slot that is free. Customer searches are never refused to make room for optional work, although they can be refused when all eight slots are busy and their 250-millisecond queue is full. Within the optional allowance, exports yield first. An export is admitted only while fewer than five shared slots are busy, whereas a suggestion is admitted while fewer than six are busy, because a customer is waiting for the suggestion and an export can resume later. These occupancy checks are not atomic, so concurrent requests can pass them using the same reading, but the semaphores limit optional work to two concurrent calls regardless, so such a race cannot reduce the capacity protected for customer searches. Chapter 14 applies the same structure to payment-provider capacity, where captures, refunds, and reconciliation hold reserved calls.

Table \(\ref{tab:guardrail-reduced-responses}\) lists other reduced responses and the work each one avoids. Two rules apply to all of them. Deferred work grows the backlog if producers keep sending at the same rate, so every queue needs a limit, and financial records and required audit events can never inherit the omission policy of optional analytics. Priority must also be assigned by a trusted rule on the server, because if callers could mark their own work as urgent, every caller would, and the reservation would protect nothing.

Implementing Admission Checks

Every policy in this chapter depends on admission checks that reserve capacity atomically, and one mistake occurs in many implementations. If several requests read an in-flight gauge showing seven active calls against a limit of eight, each concludes that a slot is free, and all of them proceed. This mistake is known as check-then-act, because each request reasons correctly about a number that has changed by the time it acts. A semaphore prevents it by allowing exactly one request to acquire the final permit.

An export query needs two permits, an optional-work permit and a shared backend permit, and Listing \(\ref{lst:ch09-admission}\) acquires them without blocking. If the shared permit is unavailable, the optional-work permit is released and the request follows its refusal or deferral policy. The client and deadline interfaces in the listing are illustrative.

from threading import BoundedSemaphore

optional_slots = BoundedSemaphore(2)   # exports and suggestions
backend_slots = BoundedSemaphore(8)

def fetch_export_page(query, deadline):
    if not optional_slots.acquire(blocking=False):
        raise ExportCapacityUnavailable()

    try:
        if not backend_slots.acquire(blocking=False):
            raise SearchCapacityUnavailable()

        try:
            deadline.require_time_for_attempt()

            return search_client.fetch_page(
                query=query,
                deadline=deadline,
            )
        finally:
            backend_slots.release()
    finally:
        optional_slots.release()

Suggestions acquire the same two permits through their own function, and customer searches acquire only the shared backend permit. Because each process holds its own semaphore objects, these numbers are local limits, and the fleet total depends on the allocation in Table \(\ref{tab:search-allocation}\). The client call must also finish its local work before the function returns, because a call that returned a future while execution continued would release its permits too early.

A local permit cannot confirm that the remote query has stopped. If the client gives up at its deadline while the cluster continues executing the query, releasing the permit lets a new query start alongside the old one, and a process can then have more than eight queries running in the cluster. The fleet allocation therefore holds only if the cluster enforces its own query timeout close to the client’s deadline, and the team verified that canceling a query on the client stops it on the cluster, using the cancellation behavior described in Chapter 4. The breaker and rate limiter must also be combined with the semaphores carefully. If a half-open probe receives permission from the breaker but cannot acquire a backend slot, the implementation must return that permission without recording a failed call. Errors in cancellation and partial admission like these can leak permits slowly or admit more work than the configuration allows, so each deserves its own test.

State-Changing Operations

Refusing a search has no side effects, because a search only reads data. Operations that change money, inventory, or order state are harder, because a refusal before dispatch and a lost response after dispatch mean opposite things. A refusal before dispatch shows that the operation did not start, whereas a lost response leaves the caller unable to tell whether it completed. If a bulkhead rejects an authorization request, another request for the same operation may already be running, so the response must consult the durable operation state before telling the customer that no payment was submitted. A timeout after an outbound write likewise requires reconciliation under the original operation identifier, as described in Chapter 3, because a new identifier created to get around a breaker or retry limit would also bypass the protection against duplicate effects. Status lookups and recovery work need bounded allocations of their own, so that blocking new writes never prevents a customer from checking an accepted operation, and so that recovery cannot consume unlimited dependency capacity merely because it is important.

Calibration and Recovery Testing

By this point, the search application had several limits that interacted with one another, and the team needed to know whether they would work together, especially during recovery, when queued exports and delayed retries would compete with returning customer traffic. One option was to make the limits adaptive, adjusting them automatically from measured latency. Adaptive limits make sense when available capacity varies widely, but a controller that reacts to every latency sample tends to oscillate, raising and lowering admission repeatedly, and a stable one needs measurement windows, bounded adjustments, separate conditions for lowering and restoring limits, and a policy for stale data. Because the search cluster’s capacity was stable, fixed and tested limits and a way to pause exports gave the team the containment it needed without that complexity.

The SLO indicators from Chapter 8 show the customer consequences of these limits, but they should not drive admission on their own, because rejected requests count against the SLO. A rule that rejected more requests whenever the burn rate rose would reinforce the condition that triggered it.

A Practical Test Plan

The test begins with representative customer searches, suggestions, and a realistic mix of catalog sizes for exports. The load generator sends requests at a fixed arrival rate regardless of how quickly responses return, because a generator that waits for each response before sending the next reduces its own load as the service slows and hides the overload it was meant to create.

Exports are then added until the application reaches its configured limits, and the engineers confirm that accepted work remains bounded, that refusals are counted, and that customer searches keep their six protected slots while exports and suggestions are both at their limits. Next, cluster responses are delayed and selected calls are prevented from completing, which exercises the seconds before the breaker opens. The cluster is then restored while queued jobs and retry candidates are waiting, and the test continues until the backlog clears. If the first probes succeed and the cluster then overloads again, the staged recovery policy needs revision. Finally, the engineers repeat the relevant cases with one instance unavailable and during a deployment, because both conditions change how local limits add up across the fleet.

The test report shows accepted, completed, refused, and timed-out work, together with queue age and customer-facing latency, because latency for completed requests alone can improve merely because the application refused most of them. Each refusal is recorded with the active policy version and its reason, so that an engineer who sees refusals rise can tell whether they came from the merchant quota, the optional-work allowance, the shared backend limit, or an open breaker.

::: fieldnote

**Amazon S3, February 2017**

On February 28, 2017, an authorized Amazon S3 engineer was investigating slow responses in the S3 billing system in the US-EAST-1 region. An incorrect input to a command intended to remove a small number of servers removed far more than intended, including servers supporting the index and placement subsystems, on which every S3 request in the region depended. Both subsystems had to be fully restarted, and because they had grown substantially since their last full restart, recovery took much longer than expected.

AWS changed the tool to remove capacity more slowly and to refuse any removal that would take a subsystem below its minimum required capacity. Like the admission limits in this chapter, these checks bound the consequences of a mistake rather than trying to prevent every mistake. The long restart teaches a separate lesson, which is that a recovery procedure should be tested at the scale at which it will be needed in production.

Source: published incident report.

:::

Summary

Catalog exports and customer searches competed for one pool of application workers and one search cluster. The first limit caused customers to queue behind long exports; the second allowed export queries to increase the execution time of searches already admitted. Separating the worker executors addressed the first problem. Reserving backend capacity by workload, with a tested fleet-wide allocation, addressed the second.

Moving exports to queued jobs removed long waits from the synchronous request, but required backlog admission, cancellation, and recovery. When the search cluster slowed for every caller during an index rebuild, the team added a circuit breaker, rate limits, and a bounded retry policy. The recovery test mattered as much as the outage test: resuming exports and delayed retries all at once could have overloaded the recovering cluster again.

Local semaphores restrict dispatch from one process. They cannot prove that a remote query has stopped after a client timeout, and their sum may exceed the intended fleet allocation during a deployment surge. The cluster’s own execution timeout and the deployment’s maximum instance count must support the limit that the application claims to enforce. Chapter 10 examines release changes that can invalidate those assumptions while still returning correct results.

::: hiddenassumptions

Assumption and scope & Interactive search, suggestions, and merchant exports can share execution resources because they use the same backend API.
Condition that tests it & Export demand or slow cluster responses consume the shared execution slots.
Constraint or invariant & Export jobs, export queries, and the job backlog have separate limits. Exports and suggestions share a two-slot optional allowance inside the eight shared slots, every process counts toward fleet usage, and background callers enforce a combined reservation of 16.
Evidence and uncertainty & Concurrency tests that vary only backend permits, with suggestions active, compare search latency with export throughput. Catalog size, uneven traffic, deployment overlap, and queries that continue after client cancellation can all change resource usage.
Signal and evaluation window & Interactive latency, permit use, rejected work, and breaker samples, measured over each overload test.
Control and decision & Limit export jobs before they are queued, protect customer searches from optional work, refuse new jobs when the backlog cannot meet the promised completion time, and resume deferred work in stages after recovery.
Owner and review trigger & The search team owns backend-call policy, the merchant-feature owner defines export acceptance and completion commitments, and the platform team verifies shared capacity and deployment accounting. Review after an overload or dependency failure, and before expanding exports to more merchants.
:::
